blocks.body:
In 1742 Goldbach and Euler corresponded about writing numbers as sums of primes. In modern form, the binary conjecture says every even number greater than $2$ is a sum of two primes. The ternary (or weak) conjecture says every odd number greater than $5$ is a sum of three primes:
$$N = p_1+p_2+p_3 \qquad (N > 5 \text{ odd}).$$
The binary statement implies the ternary one. If $N \ge 9$ is odd, then $N-3$ is even and at least $6$, so $N - 3 = p+p'$ and $N = 3+p+p'$. Together with $7 = 2+2+3$ this covers everything. The binary conjecture is still open. The ternary one was proved in two stages: Vinogradov (1937) for all sufficiently large odd $N$, and Helfgott (2013) for every odd $N>5$.

blocks.title: Setting up the circle method
blocks.body:
Weight each prime by $\log p$ and count
$$R(N) = \sum_{p_1+p_2+p_3=N}\log p_1\log p_2\log p_3 = \int_0^1 S(\alpha)^3e(-N\alpha)\,d\alpha, \qquad S(\alpha) = \sum_{p\le N}(\log p)\,e(p\alpha).$$
This is the [[circle-method]] with $\mathcal A$ = the primes. The plan is to show $R(N) \sim \mathfrak S(N)N^2/2$ with $\mathfrak S(N)$ bounded below for odd $N$. Then $R(N) > 0$, so representations exist.

Near a rational $a/q$, split the primes by residue class mod $q$. Only classes $r$ with $\gcd(r,q)=1$ contain more than one prime. Each class carries about a $1/\varphi(q)$ share of the weight, by the prime number theorem in progressions, and its primes all have phase $e(ar/q)$. So
$$S\Bigl(\frac aq\Bigr) \approx \frac{N}{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\substack{r=1\\ (r,q)=1}}^{q}e\Bigl(\frac{ar}{q}\Bigr) = \frac{\mu(q)}{\varphi(q)}N .$$
The last step uses the Ramanujan sum evaluation below. For this approximation to hold uniformly for $q$ up to a power of $\log N$, one needs the [[siegel-walfisz|Siegel–Walfisz theorem]]. That is the source of the ineffective constant in Vinogradov's theorem.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Multiplying by $a$ permutes the residues prime to $q$, so $c_q(a) = c_q(1)$. Detect the condition $\gcd(r,q)=1$ with $\sum_{d\mid \gcd(r,q)}\mu(d)$, as in [[mobius|Möbius inversion]]:
$$c_q(1) = \sum_{d\mid q}\mu(d)\sum_{\substack{r=1\\ d\mid r}}^{q}e\Bigl(\frac rq\Bigr) = \sum_{d\mid q}\mu(d)\sum_{s=1}^{q/d}e\Bigl(\frac{s}{q/d}\Bigr).$$
The inner sum is a full sum of $(q/d)$-th roots of unity. It is $0$ unless $q/d = 1$, in which case it is $1$. Only $d = q$ survives, which leaves $\mu(q)$. $\square$

blocks.title: Major arcs: the singular series
blocks.body:
Integrating the approximation over the major arcs (short intervals around $a/q$ with $q \le (\log N)^B$) gives the main term
$$\mathfrak S(N)\cdot\frac{N^2}{2}, \qquad \mathfrak S(N) = \sum_{q=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu(q)}{\varphi(q)^3}\,c_q(-N) .$$
Here $\mu(q)^3 = \mu(q)$, and the $N^2/2$ comes from $\binom{N-1}{2}$, the number of ways to write $N$ as a sum of three positive integers. The terms are multiplicative in $q$ and supported on squarefree $q$, so the series is an Euler product. At a prime, $c_p(-N) = p-1$ if $p\mid N$ and $-1$ otherwise, so
$$\mathfrak S(N) = \prod_{p\mid N}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\Bigr)\prod_{p\nmid N}\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{(p-1)^3}\Bigr).$$
The factor at $p=2$ is $0$ when $N$ is even and $2$ when $N$ is odd. So for odd $N$,
$$\mathfrak S(N) \ge 2\prod_{p\ge3}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\Bigr) = 2C_2 \approx 1.3203,$$
where $C_2 \approx 0.66016$ is the twin prime constant. The singular series sees the parity obstruction and nothing else.

blocks.title: Minor arcs: Vinogradov's estimate
blocks.body:
On the rest of $[0,1]$, Dirichlet's approximation theorem gives every $\alpha$ a rational $a/q$ with $|\alpha-a/q| \le q^{-2}$ and $(\log N)^B < q \le N(\log N)^{-B}$. Vinogradov's key estimate, in the form later simplified using Vaughan's identity, is
$$S(\alpha) \ll \Bigl(\frac{N}{\sqrt q}+N^{4/5}+\sqrt{Nq}\Bigr)(\log N)^4 \qquad\text{whenever } \Bigl|\alpha-\frac aq\Bigr|\le\frac1{q^2},\ \gcd(a,q)=1 .$$
On the minor arcs this gives $|S(\alpha)| \ll N(\log N)^{4-B/2}$. With Parseval, $\int_0^1|S|^2 = \sum_{p\le N}(\log p)^2 \le \theta(N)\log N \ll N\log N$, so
$$\Bigl|\int_{\mathfrak m}S(\alpha)^3e(-N\alpha)\,d\alpha\Bigr| \le \sup_{\mathfrak m}|S|\int_0^1|S|^2 \ll N^2(\log N)^{5-B/2},$$
which is $o(N^2)$ once $B>10$. We do not prove the minor arc estimate. Its proof is a bilinear-form argument, close in spirit to the one behind [[bombieri-vinogradov]].

blocks.title: Vinogradov's three primes theorem (1937)
blocks.body:
For every $A > 0$,
$$R(N) = \mathfrak S(N)\frac{N^2}{2} + O_A\Bigl(\frac{N^2}{(\log N)^A}\Bigr).$$
Hence every sufficiently large odd $N$ is a sum of three primes, and the number of ordered representations is asymptotic to $\mathfrak S(N)N^2/(2(\log N)^3)$.

blocks.title: From sufficiently large to every N
blocks.body:
Siegel's theorem makes the constant in Siegel–Walfisz ineffective, so Vinogradov's original argument did not say how large $N$ must be. Later versions made it explicit, but the thresholds were astronomically large, far beyond any computer check. Two routes closed the gap.

1. Conditionally: Hardy and Littlewood (1923) had already proved the result for large $N$ assuming the generalised Riemann hypothesis. Deshouillers, Effinger, te Riele and Zinoviev (1997) completed it for all odd $N>5$ under GRH, with a computation.
2. Unconditionally: Helfgott (2013) sharpened both arcs dramatically, with explicit, carefully optimised estimates, and brought the threshold down to a size that could be checked. The remaining range was covered by rigorous computation. This included, with D. Platt, a verification of the ternary statement beyond $10^{30}$, and checks of zeros of Dirichlet $L$-functions of small modulus up to a finite height.

blocks.title: Ternary Goldbach (Helfgott, 2013)
blocks.body: Every odd integer $N>5$ can be written as $N = p_1+p_2+p_3$ with $p_1,p_2,p_3$ prime.

blocks.title: Small cases
blocks.body: Check the theorem for the first few odd numbers, and for all odd $N$ with $7\le N\le 10^4$.
blocks.solution:
$7 = 2+2+3$, $9 = 3+3+3$, $11 = 3+3+5$, $13 = 3+3+7$, $15 = 3+5+7$.

For odd $N$ with $9 \le N \le 10^4$ one can always take $p_1 = 3$, because $N-3$ is an even number between $6$ and $10^4$, and every such number is a sum of two primes (binary Goldbach has been checked by computer far beyond this range). A direct search confirms this. In this range $N = 7$ is the only case that needs the prime $2$: three odd primes add up to at least $3+3+3 = 9$, so $7$ must use $2$, and $7 = 2+2+3$ is the only way.

blocks.title: Four primes for even numbers
blocks.body: Deduce from the theorem that every even integer $N\ge8$ is a sum of four primes, and that every integer $N \ge 2$ is a sum of at most four primes.
blocks.solution:
If $N \ge 8$ is even, then $N-2$ is odd and at least $6$, hence at least $7$. By Helfgott's theorem $N-2 = p_1+p_2+p_3$, so $N = 2+p_1+p_2+p_3$.

For the second claim: $2,3,5$ are primes, $4 = 2+2$, $6 = 3+3$, odd $N\ge7$ need three primes, and even $N \ge 8$ need at most four. So four primes always suffice. Binary Goldbach would bring this down to three.

blocks.title: Singular series in practice
blocks.body: Evaluate $\mathfrak S(N)$ for $N = 10001 = 73\cdot137$, and compare the prediction $\mathfrak S(N)N^2/2$ with the exact weighted count $R(N)$.
blocks.solution:
Since $N$ is odd, the factor at $2$ is $2$. The primes dividing $N$ are $73$ and $137$, with factors $1-1/72^2$ and $1-1/136^2$. Every other odd prime contributes $1+1/(p-1)^3$. Multiplying out (the product converges quickly), $\mathfrak S(10001) \approx 2.3004$. The prediction is $\mathfrak S(N)N^2/2 \approx 1.1504\times10^8$.

A direct enumeration of ordered triples of primes summing to $10001$ finds $255348$ triples, with total weight $R(10001) \approx 0.960\cdot\mathfrak S(N)N^2/2$. The ratio approaches $1$ slowly, as the error term suggests.

The unweighted number of triples is not well predicted by $\mathfrak S(N)N^2/(2(\log N)^3) \approx 1.47\times10^5$ at this size. The weights $\log p_i$ vary a lot over $[2,N]$, and replacing them by $\log N$ is only accurate in the limit. This is why analytic number theorists prefer weighted counts.

blocks.body:
- Vinogradov's 1937 theorem is for sufficiently large $N$ only. Do not quote it as proving the full conjecture. That needed Helfgott's explicit work plus computation.
- The singular series vanishes for even $N$, but that does not make $R(N)$ zero. Triples containing the prime $2$, such as $2+p+q$, can occur. Their total weight is $O(N(\log N)^2)$, of lower order than $N^2$, which is why the main term does not see them.
- The ternary method does not adapt to two primes. The minor arc argument needs a spare factor $S(\alpha)$ for the supremum, and with two factors the trivial mean square is already as large as the main term.
- The $\log$-weighted count $R(N)$ and the plain count differ by roughly a factor $(\log N)^3$ only asymptotically. Numerically the two can differ noticeably.

Ternary Goldbach is the showcase of the [[circle-method]] for primes. Its major arcs rest on [[siegel-walfisz]] and the minor arcs on [[exponential-sums]] over primes. The binary problem, [[goldbach]], remains open. The best results there are Chen's theorem, a sieve result that uses [[bombieri-vinogradov]], and the circle-method theorem that almost all even numbers are sums of two primes. The singular series here is a cousin of the constants in the Hardy–Littlewood conjectures on [[twin-primes]] and [[prime-patterns]].

1. Show that $\mathfrak S(N) = \sum_q \mu(q)c_q(-N)/\varphi(q)^3$ converges absolutely, using $|c_q(N)| \le \gcd(q,N)$ for squarefree $q$.
2. Compute $c_{12}(5)$ and $c_{6}(3)$ directly from the definition.
3. Show that the number of ordered triples of positive integers summing to $N$ is $\binom{N-1}{2}$.
4. Explain why the factor at $p=3$ in $\mathfrak S(N)$ is smaller when $3\mid N$ than when $3\nmid N$, by counting solutions of $x+y+z\equiv N \pmod 3$ with $x,y,z \not\equiv 0$.
